design_detail: Mixed-methods systematic review without meta-analysis (not preregistered; sequential explanatory design following the Cochrane adverse-effects framework) of adverse events during and after clinical treatment of patients with MDMA or serotonergic psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca). PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE and PsycINFO searched on 28 July 2021 for studies published since 2000, plus ClinicalTrials.gov to cross-check publications, handsearching and reference lists. 44 articles (34 quantitative, 10 qualitative) on 598 unique patients; for MDMA 16 studies (one qualitative) with 266 patients treated. Adverse events grouped as acute (day of session) or late; prevalence recalculated as a percentage of participants; qualitative studies used to contextualize. No formal risk-of-bias assessment by design. Academic review (University of Groningen and partners).
can_establish: Which acute and late adverse events the clinical MDMA studies published up to mid-2021 reported, in which populations, and how (in)completely they assessed them.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA causes these events (no pooling, few controlled comparisons, no risk-of-bias appraisal), how often rare or delayed harms occur, or harms in unselected patients; for PTSD its main data come from a pooled phase 2 analysis since retracted.

sample.recruitment: Database search on 28 July 2021 (5640 records, 3709 after deduplication, screened independently by two authors; 61 full texts assessed; 44 included); 596 registered trials found, 24 completed trials included (Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1, an image).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: quantitative and qualitative clinical studies, from case reports to randomized trials, published since 2000, of patients with a (mental) disorder treated with a classic serotonergic psychedelic or an entactogen; no further exclusion criteria set in advance. Excluded: systematic reviews, surveys, secondary analyses and studies in healthy volunteers (Methods › Selection criteria).
sample.demographics: Studies published 2006 to 2021; samples of 1 to 105 (mean 23); mean ages 25 to 59; 521 of the 598 received an active dose (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Most included trials had strict eligibility criteria and many participants with prior experience of the drug (up to 56% for MDMA; Limitations). The review excludes secondary analyses but uses the pooled phase 2 analysis by Mithoefer et al. (2019) as its main PTSD source.

exposure.measurement: Study drug as given in each included study (Table 1): MDMA in one to three sessions, with psychotherapy in all MDMA studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed in Table 1: oral MDMA from 50 to 125 mg (with optional supplemental half doses in several studies); the tinnitus trial 30 against 70 mg in one session.
exposure.polysubstance: Prior MDMA or ecstasy use extracted: from none (Danforth 2018) to 56% (Wolfson 2020); not reported in six MDMA studies (Quality appraisal under MDMA).

comparison.controls: Whatever the primary studies used: inactive placebo, low-dose MDMA (0 to 40 mg in the pooled phase 2 PTSD row), none in open-label studies. No pooled comparison.

outcomes.instruments: Adverse events as each study recorded them: mostly spontaneous reports and therapist observation; a few structured instruments (C-SSRS, UKU side-effect scale, Challenging Experience Questionnaire); CASP for the qualitative studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review defines an adverse event as any unfavourable or harmful event first occurring during or after administration, regardless of relationship to the treatment, and distinguishes only acute and late events.
outcomes.operationalization: Prevalence of each reported event as a percentage of participants, per study and arm; the 3 to 5 most reported events shown in Table 1, all in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts screened independently by two authors; data extraction by one author (BWK), discussed with two others; all articles read by the first author.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. For MDMA (Table 1 and text): in the pooled phase 2 PTSD row (taken from the since-retracted Mithoefer et al., 2019; MDMA n = 72, control n = 31) acute anxiety 72% against 48%, jaw clenching 64% against 19%, lack of appetite 49% against 23%, nausea 40% against 19%, but fatigue 49% against 58% and headache 53% against 71%; in the life-threatening-illness trial (Wolfson 2020; MDMA 13, placebo 5) acute jaw clenching 85% against 20%, thirst 85% against 40%, perspiration 69% against none; in the autism social-anxiety trial (Danforth 2018; MDMA 8, placebo 4) acute anxiety 75% against 25%. One MDMA-related serious adverse event: an increase in pre-existing premature ventricular contractions requiring one night of hospital monitoring (Mithoefer 2018).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The review was not preregistered (Methods, 1st paragraph); it calls its approach exploratory.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the 3 to 5 most reported events per study appear in the article; the full list is in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors note that small samples may miss less frequent events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across small, mostly uncontrolled or poorly blinded clinical studies, MDMA was followed by common transient acute events (jaw clenching or muscle tightness, headache, nausea, fatigue, reduced appetite, feeling cold, anxiety) and late events in the following days (fatigue, low mood, insomnia, anxiety, difficulty concentrating), with one MDMA-related serious adverse event; adverse events were rarely assessed systematically and four quantitative studies reported none.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say that MDMA and psychedelics appear to be well tolerated, with caution; the Conclusions add that serious adverse events seem largely absent. The authors themselves state that adverse events are probably under-reported because of design and sample selection, which limits how much 'well tolerated' can mean.

timeline.event: Colcott et al. meta-analysis across indications cites this review and finds a similar pattern of common transient side effects and poor harms reporting.
10 August 2024: the pooled phase 2 analysis used here for the PTSD trials (Mithoefer et al., 2019) is retracted.

replication.where_it_stands: A broad descriptive map of reported adverse events, consistent in direction with the later meta-analysis, but its PTSD figures rest on a retracted pooled analysis and it has no risk-of-bias appraisal. Cite it for the non-PTSD trials' reported events and for the state of harms assessment, not for the PTSD pooled figures.

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: RS received a research grant from the Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development for an oral esketamine study, is co-investigator of a psilocybin study funded by Compass Pathways, and received an educational grant from Janssen and an honorarium from Clexio Biosciences. EV is principal investigator of an MDMA trial funded by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies. WvdB has consulted for Janssen Netherlands and is on the Scientific Advisory Board of Clearmind. JJB, BK and JK declare none.
funding.affiliations_note: Eric Vermetten, principal investigator of a MAPS-funded MDMA trial, is also a co-author of the sponsor's pooled sleep analysis (Ponte et al., 2021).

what_would_settle_it: Trials of MDMA-assisted therapy that assess adverse events prospectively with structured instruments at fixed times (sessions, following week, months later), report severity, timing and relatedness by arm, and include people with the comorbidity seen in practice.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items fail: no registered protocol (2) and no risk-of-bias assessment (9); item 7 is provisional (supplements not read) but cannot change the rating. The review is a careful descriptive map of what studies reported, explicitly exploratory, and can be cited for which adverse events were reported in which trials and for how poorly they were assessed. Its PTSD figures come from a pooled analysis retracted in 2024 and must not be cited.

key_findings.finding: 44 articles (34 quantitative, 10 qualitative) on 598 unique patients, 521 of whom received an active dose; studies published 2006 to 2021; sample sizes 1 to 105 (mean 23); four quantitative and two qualitative studies did not report on adverse events.

MDMA: 16 studies including one qualitative (266 patients treated). PTSD: 10 publications (214 patients), seven RCTs (Mitchell 2021; Mithoefer 2011, 2013b, 2018, 2019; Oehen 2013; Ot'alora 2018), one open-label trial, one couples case series, one qualitative study. Other indications: RCTs in end-of-life anxiety (Wolfson 2020), social anxiety in autistic adults (Danforth 2018) and tinnitus (Searchfield 2020); an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (Sessa 2019, 2021).

The PTSD phase 2 data in Table 1 come from one merged row headed by the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (Mithoefer et al., 2019) together with the individual trials: 105 participants (MDMA 72, control 31 on 0 to 40 mg).
key_findings.note: Mithoefer et al. (2019) was retracted on 10 August 2024 (PMC marks it); these figures must not be cited.

key_findings.finding: Assessment: 11 MDMA studies recorded adverse events only when spontaneously reported; one did not report them (tinnitus); two RCTs assessed them systematically (Mitchell 2021; the pooled phase 2 analysis); prior MDMA or ecstasy use not reported in six studies and ranging from none to 56% in the others.

Physiological: nine MDMA studies measured blood pressure, temperature and heart rate; all reported mild, transient, statistically significant elevations during sessions, none needing medical intervention. One MDMA-related serious adverse event: an increase in pre-existing premature ventricular contractions requiring one night of hospital monitoring, resolving spontaneously (Mithoefer 2018).

PTSD: most common acute events jaw clenching or tight muscles, headache, nausea, fatigue and lack of appetite, and anxiety as the main psychological event; serious adverse events in two studies: suicidal behaviour and suicidal ideation leading to self-hospitalization, only in the control group (Mitchell 2021); in Mithoefer 2018 three of four serious events considered unrelated and one (premature ventricular contractions) potentially related.
key_findings.locator: Results › MDMA › Adverse events › PTSD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Life-threatening illness (Wolfson 2020; MDMA 13, placebo 5): acute jaw clenching 11 (85%) against 1 (20%), thirst 11 (85%) against 2 (40%), dry mouth 9 (69%) against 1 (20%), perspiration 9 (69%) against none, headache 8 (62%) against 1 (20%); in the next 7 days fatigue 92% against 60%, anxiety 62% against 40%, low mood 46% against 60%; treatment-emergent anxiety, depression and dissociation (1 each) only with MDMA; no serious adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, MDMA › Other disorders, Wolfson et al. (2020) row; Results › MDMA › Adverse events › End-of-life anxiety

key_findings.finding: Autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018; MDMA 8, placebo 4): acute anxiety 6 (75%) against 1 (25%), difficulty concentrating 63% against 25%; after the first session depressed mood, suicidal ideation and panic in two of eight MDMA and one of four placebo participants; no serious adverse events.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Danforth et al. (2018) row; Results › MDMA › Adverse events › Social anxiety

key_findings.finding: Across MDMA studies the commonest late events were fatigue, headache, anxiety, difficulty concentrating and low mood; low mood occurred in both MDMA and placebo groups; suicidal ideation and behaviour were reported in three MDMA studies at rates lower than or similar to controls, with serious events only in control groups.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Late AEs, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Suicidality

key_findings.finding: The authors report press accounts of MDMA trial participants who said they became suicidal after a trial, including a participant who remained attached to a therapist and was abused (Lindsay, 2022; Rosin, 2022, news sources), and call for systematic monitoring of adverse effects.

Limitations named by the authors: mostly small and heterogeneous studies; few with systematic or consistent assessment; not enough placebo-controlled trials for causal conclusions; severity and timing rarely reported; strict eligibility; prior drug experience up to 56% for MDMA; under-representation of minorities.

reporting_issues.issue: The review excludes secondary analyses, yet its main PTSD data come from a pooled secondary analysis of six phase 2 trials (Mithoefer et al., 2019), merged with the individual trials into one row; that analysis was retracted in August 2024.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Selection criteria; Table 1, PTSD third row; Results › MDMA, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The PTSD phase 2 percentages in Table 1 and the late-event figures for 'this group' (17, 6 and 4 of 72) must not be cited; other rows are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The text attributes the use of the UKU side-effect scale and the only report of adverse-event severity to Oehen et al. (2013), but Table 1 lists the UKU scale for Bouso et al. (2008).

reporting_issues.consequence: Which study measured severity is unclear; minor for claims.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say four quantitative studies did not report on adverse events, the Limitations say five pilot studies did not report any (including Bouso 2008 and Sessa 2021b), while Table 1 lists adverse events for Bouso 2008 and an abnormal rise in blood pressure for Sessa 2021; the text also says the alcohol use disorder study did not report on adverse events.
